title.narrative: Gemensamt FN-program mot könsstympning av flickor och kvinnor
Joint UN Programme on Eliminating FGM, Phase IV

description.narrative:
Det övergripande målet för programmet är att utrota könsstympning av flickor och kvinnor till 2030 i enlighet med SDG mål 5.3. Det långsiktiga resultatet för programmet är: nya och mer rättvisa sociala normer som utrotar skadliga normer och underliggande drivkrafter till könsstympning och ojämlikhet mellan könen.
Resultaten på medellång sikt är: - Flickors och kvinnors egenmakt har stärkts, de känner till och hävdar rätten till sin kropp och driver tillsammans med anhöriga och andra nyckelaktörer förändringar av sociala normer och könsnormer. - Flickor och kvinnor har tillgång till allsidiga och kvalitativa samhällstjänster såsom hälso- och sjukvård, utbildning och juridiskt stöd för att förebygga och hantera konsekvenser könsstympning. - Ökat ansvarsutkrävande av regeringar och andra duty bearers inklusive ökade resurser för sektorsövergripande politik, lagar och ramverk för att tillhandahålla förebyggande insatser för kvinnor och flickor som riskerar utsättas för könsstympning även i svåråtkomliga/avlägsna områden.

The overall objective (impact) of the program is: The global promise of ending female genital mutilation is delivered by 2030.
The long term outcome is: Emergence of new and more equitable social norms transforming all harmful practices that drive FGM and gender inequality.
The medium term outcomes are:
- Empowered girls and women know and claim rights to their bodily autonomy and, together with their families and communities, drive changes in social and gender norms. - Girls and women can access a comprehensive package of high quality, gender-responsive, disability-inclusive, culturally and age appropriate services from relevant sectoral systems and institutions. - Governments and other duty-bearers demonstrate increased accountability for resourcing and implementing multi-sectoral policies, laws and frameworks to provide prevention and response for women and girls at risk of, and affected by, FGM - even in hard-to-reach locations.
The short-term outcomes are:
- Girls and women demonstrating increased assets, capabilities and agency in relation to their rights to bodily integrity, gender equitable roles and relationships. - Men, boys, families and communities increasingly supporting the access of women and girls to measures and services that prevent and protect them against FGM, gender inequalities and other harmful practices. -Health, education, social, legal and child protection systems providing integrated quality FGM services that are accessible and centred on women and girls, as well as families and communities. - A broad range of actors at the global, regional, national and local levels, amplifying their collective efforts to advocate, develop, implement, monitor and evaluate gender transformative multi-sectoral evidence-based FGM elimination policy and legal frameworks with adequate resourcing.

sector.narrative: Ending violence against women and girls

description.narrative:
The 2025 Annual report captures the following results I. Changing Attitudes and Social Norms The report shows a gradual but important shift in how female genital mutilation (FGM) is understood and discussed. While the practice still affects more than 200 million women and girls globally, according to UNICEF, there is growing recognition in several countries that FGM is harmful rather than simply a cultural tradition. In places such as Côte dIvoire, public discussions have become more open, and more people are beginning to question the practice.
Survey data from multiple highprevalence countries indicates that a majority of women now believe FGM should end. This change in perception is critical because the practice is largely sustained by social pressure. As more individuals begin to reject it, the collective expectation that once upheld it begins to weaken, creating space for change.
II. Stronger Legal Protection and Use of the Courts The report highlights clear progress in how laws are being used to protect girls. More than 25 countries where FGM is practiced now have laws banning it, but enforcement has often been inconsistent. During the period under review (2025), there are signs that this is improving.
In Kenya, the High Court upheld the national law prohibiting FGM, reinforcing the responsibility of the state to act against the practice. In another case, international intervention prevented the deportation of a girl from Denmark who faced a real risk of FGM. These examples show that legal systems are not only in place, but are increasingly being used to prevent harm and protect individuals directly.
III. Increased Government Responsibility and Oversight Governments are showing stronger engagement in addressing FGM. National institutions, including parliaments, are paying closer attention to how policies are implemented and whether commitments are being fulfilled. In some countries, this includes reviewing budgets to ensure that funding is allocated to efforts aimed at ending FGM.
Although spending levels differ widely, this growing focus on accountability marks an important step forward. It shows that FGM is being treated less as a peripheral issue and more as a priority that requires consistent and coordinated government action.
IV. Regional Cooperation Across Borders FGM often continues across national borders, as families move girls to places where laws are weaker or less enforced. The report highlights progress in addressing this challenge through increased cooperation between countries.
In East Africa, five countries have worked together to develop and begin implementing a joint plan to address crossborder FGM. Regional bodies such as the African Union have supported these efforts, helping countries align their approaches. This kind of cooperation is essential for closing gaps that allow the practice to continue despite national bans.
V. CommunityLed Action and Local Monitoring At the community level, there are encouraging signs of change that go beyond policy and law. In several areas, communities that have publicly committed to ending FGM are now taking steps to ensure those commitments are upheld.
This includes setting up local monitoring systems and involving community leaders in discouraging the practice. Evidence from countries such as Ethiopia and Senegal shows that when communities collectively abandon FGM, prevalence can decline significantly within a generation. These efforts are important because change is more likely to last when it is led by the communities themselves.
VI. Greater Use of International Platforms Another key development is the increased use of international platforms to push for action. Civil society groups are making more effective use of global review processes to highlight gaps and hold governments accountable.
As a result, governments are receiving more detailed recommendations and, in some cases, responding with concrete steps. This stronger link between global discussions and national action is helping to maintain attention on FGM and encourage progress.
VII. Measurable Progress and Remaining Challenges The report reflects both immediate and longer term progress. In the short term, there have been direct actions that protect individuals, strengthen laws, and support policy development. Over time, there are signs of deeper change, including shifting attitudes, stronger institutions, and improved cooperation.
However, challenges remain. Progress is uneven, and in some regions particularly parts of East and West AfricaFGM prevalence can still exceed 70% in certain communities. Not all countries are making full use of the tools available to them, and responses are sometimes slow.
Overall, the findings show a steady movement in the right direction. While the numbers remain high, the combination of changing attitudes, stronger laws, increased government action, and community involvement is beginning to create the conditions needed for a sustained decline in FGM and, ultimately, its elimination.
